title: Nonprofit and Volunteer-Group Basics in Canada
summary: By the end, learners can tell an informal volunteer group from an Alberta society, a CRA registered charity, and an Alberta “charitable organization,” describe what a society can and cannot do, outline the official map for incorporating a society, and know that only a CRA registered charity can issue official donation tax receipts.

lessons.title: A volunteer group is not automatically a charity
lessons.html:
Many community projects start as a few neighbours who want to run a supper, a rink, or a fundraiser. That informal group can do a great deal. It is not, by itself, a legal society or a registered charity.

The Government of Alberta says the words non-profit and charity are often used as if they mean the same thing, but they do not. Incorporating as a non-profit, being a registered charity with the Canada Revenue Agency, and being a charitable organization registered in Alberta are not the same. They require different processes. A group may choose one of these statuses, or more than one.

Before you start a new organization, Alberta asks you to consider a few questions. Has another group already taken on this problem? What value would a new organization add? Have you looked at the need? Could you partner with a group that already exists? How would the organization be supported financially? There may already be an organization you could join or work with.

In Alberta, groups that want to incorporate can do so under different provincial or federal acts. Alberta’s Societies Act is one of the most common choices for becoming a society. Incorporation has costs and paperwork, but it can give the group a legal identity, some protection for board members who act properly, and better access to grants that must be awarded to an incorporated organization rather than to individual board members.

This course maps those official differences. It does not tell you which structure to choose, and it does not write your documents for you.

lessons.title: What an Alberta society is
lessons.html:
A society is an independent legal entity — a corporate “person” that exists separate from its members. Because of that, Alberta says the members cannot be held personally responsible for the debts of the society.

Societies are similar to non-profit companies. They must direct any profits back into fulfilling the objectives of the organization. You should get legal advice if you are not sure whether a society or a non-profit company is best for your group’s purposes.

Five or more people can form a society for purposes such as social activities, recreation, culture, or charity. You cannot form a society to carry out trade or business.

A society can buy, sell, and own property, including land. It can enter into contracts. It can sue others, and it can be sued.

A society cannot issue shares, declare dividends for members, or distribute property among the members during the lifetime of the society.

If your society plans to register as a charity under the Income Tax Act, you need to make sure the society’s objectives or purposes meet Canada Revenue Agency requirements. Becoming a society does not automatically make you a CRA registered charity.

These rules exist to keep the group’s money and property aimed at its purpose, not at paying members. They are minimum legal facts from the official page, not a full guide to running a board.

If you only need a short-term volunteer project, you may not need a society at all. If you will hold land, sign contracts, or apply for grants in the group’s name, the official page is the place to read next — and a qualified advisor is the person to ask.

lessons.title: The official map for incorporating a society
lessons.html:
Alberta publishes the steps to incorporate a society. This lesson is a map, not a do-it-yourself legal kit. Always use the live page and the current forms.

As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), the incorporation fee was $53.05. The page said to make your cheque payable to “Government of Alberta” and not to send a credit card number in the mail.

Step 1 — Choose a name. A society’s name has three parts: a distinctive element (something unique, often a place or word), a descriptive element (what the society does), and a legal element. Accepted legal elements include Society, Association, Club, Fellowship, Guild, Foundation, Institute, League, Committee, Council, Board, Centre, and Bureau. Alberta’s example is “Smith Falls White Water Rafting Association.”

Step 2 — Get an Alberta NUANS report. Review it to make sure no other society has an identical name. Identical names are not allowed. The report reserves the proposed name for 90 days and must be submitted with the incorporation details while it is still valid.

Step 3 — Fill out the forms named on the page, including an application to form a society, bylaws, and notices of address and directors.

Step 4 — Submit signed duplicates of the completed forms, the NUANS report, and the fee to Corporate Registry at the address on the live page.

If the information meets requirements, Corporate Registry mails a certificate of incorporation. You will receive an email when a federal business number is issued.

This course does not write your bylaws or choose your name. Fees and addresses can change — check the live page before you send anything.

lessons.title: A CRA registered charity is different from a non-profit
lessons.html:
The Canada Revenue Agency says registered charities and non-profit organizations (NPOs) both operate without the intention of making a profit, but they are not the same.

A registered charity is a type of qualified donee under the Income Tax Act. It may issue official donation receipts. It is established and operated for exclusively charitable purposes, and it does not pay income tax. It must use all of its resources for charitable activities that advance those purposes.

Charitable purposes fit these categories:

  • relief of poverty
  • advancement of education
  • advancement of religion
  • other purposes that benefit the community

CRA examples include food banks, schools, places of worship, animal shelters, libraries, and volunteer fire departments.

An NPO is an association, club, or society organized and operated exclusively for social welfare, civic improvement, pleasure, recreation, or any other purpose except profit. An NPO is not a qualified donee and cannot issue official donation receipts. CRA examples include some gardening clubs, book clubs, amateur sports groups, and festival organizations.

An NPO is not registered with the CRA as a charity and does not receive a charitable registration number. A registered charity must apply to become one and is issued a number. If you are operating as a charity, CRA says you cannot be considered an NPO.

Both kinds of organization generally cannot use their income to personally benefit their members (with a narrow exception on the CRA page for certain amateur-athletics groups).

Wanting to help the community is not the same as being allowed to issue a tax receipt. Only a CRA registered charity has that authority.

lessons.title: Alberta’s “charitable organization” is yet another status
lessons.html:
Alberta also uses the phrase charitable organization. That status is easy to confuse with a CRA registered charity, but Alberta says they are not the same.

Registration as a charitable organization in Alberta is done under the Charitable Fund-raising Act. It should not be confused with being a registered charity with the CRA. Alberta says this provincial registration provides a charitable registration number but does not allow the organization to write charitable donation tax receipts. Charitable status for tax purposes is granted only by the CRA.

A charitable organization must be registered under that Alberta Act if:

  • it uses a fundraising business, or
  • it intends to raise more than $25,000 in gross contributions in its financial year from solicitations to individuals in Alberta, or
  • during or after a campaign it finds it has raised more than $25,000 — in that case it must register within 45 days after contributions reach $25,000.

Those dollar figures were on the official page as of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina). Check the live page before you rely on them.

If your group later wants to become a CRA registered charity, go back to Lesson 2: the society’s purposes must meet CRA requirements, and you must apply to the CRA. Advantages Alberta lists for CRA registration include official tax receipts, income-tax exemption, and the ability to receive gifts from other registered charities.

This course cannot file your paperwork, review your purposes, or tell you that your fundraiser is “fine.” It is a map of official differences so volunteer groups do not mix up three different statuses. For a real decision, read the live pages and get legal or tax advice.
